source.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
source.authors: Maximilian Dreyer; Jim Berend; T. Labarta; Johanna Vielhaben; Thomas Wiegand; S. Lapuschkin; W. Samek

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including supplementary material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures neuron interpretability in vision models using semantic-example clarity, polysemanticity and redundancy metrics, and tests how architecture and training regularization relate to those measures. This is a different method and setting from the claim's Qwen3-32B pole audit.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test Qwen language models, positive and negative neuron poles, or the claim's percentage of poles with one or two jobs. It also does not test explanations on unseen text as in V6 or V7. Rows below concern the study's own vision-model interpretability measurements. Other results, including the neuron-labeling benchmark and medical-model correction experiments, do not measure the interpretability share described in V4 and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study scores penultimate-layer neurons in ImageNet vision models with embedding-based clarity and polysemanticity measures, which were validated against human ratings. It varies architecture, width, dropout and L1 sparsity and reports how those scores change. This bears on V4's claim that architecture and regularization, not capacity, drive messy neurons. It is a different method from the essay and gives mean scores, not shares of interpretable neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. Add that the authors attribute ViT polysemanticity to the absence of ReLU, attribute narrow-model polysemanticity to superposition in a small basis, and say transformers still need progress toward interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: This is a vision-model study using semantic embeddings of activating image examples and clarity, polysemanticity and redundancy metrics; it does not perform the claim's Qwen language-model pole audit or held-out explanation prediction test.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with architecture and training regularization; dropout effects differ between VGG and ResNet models, and L1 regularization does not improve every metric in every model.

fits_no_version.finding: Concept redundancy (overlap among neurons' semantic embeddings) rises with width and dropout and falls with L1 sparsity in most models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training regularization and width change semantic redundancy among neurons in vision models.

record.problems: The study uses vision models rather than language models. Its interpretability measures are proxies derived from a foundation model's semantic space, and the authors note dependence on that foundation model and on whether concept examples meaningfully describe a component. The paper does not turn those measures into a share of neurons with one main job. Some architecture-comparison values are available only in a figure.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise qualifying interpretability-metric results omitted. The paper's label-faithfulness comparisons, user-study correlations, task-complexity and data-augmentation experiments, and medical-model correction tests were not included because they do not measure the V4 interpretability-share claim.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B pole audit and no shares of one-job, two-job or not-understood poles.
No language or MoE models and no comparable audit shares.
No InceptionV1 cat-car neuron and no test of pose or recursive generalization versus superposition.
No share or percentage of interpretable neurons. No test that better explanation tools raise the interpretable share. No InceptionV1-sized 5% to 99% estimates. No modern LLM architectures.
Attribution graphs are shown only qualitatively, on a ResNet. There is no test of whether neurons suffice without a replacement model.
No held-out prediction of where explained neurons fire. The label-faithfulness benchmark uses synthetic images but is not framed against activating-example explanations.
No simulation-based explanation scoring on new text.

missing.what: Dropout results for ResNet34 (clarity 45.0 to 44.0, polysemanticity 91.9 to 92.3) and ResNet50 (clarity 47.1 to 47.9, polysemanticity 89.6 to 89.9): no effect
Longer training: ResNet50v2 is clearer than ResNet50 on full ImageNet, but on the subset clarity falls with epochs (e.g. ResNet34 45.7 to 43.3)
Task complexity raises clarity but also raises polysemanticity (e.g. ResNet34 85.3 to 91.9)
Wider, higher-performing models have more monosemantic units and higher alignment; VGG-16 has many polysemantic units

record.verdict_notes: These are vision CNNs and ViTs with mean proxy scores (DINOv2 embeddings), not shares of interpretable neurons. V4's 'regularization causes messiness' is ambiguous: in this paper regularization (dropout, L1) mostly improves the scores. Fig. 5b numbers are not in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit, pole-level counts, or estimates of single-job, two-job, or not-understood shares.
No language models, mixture-of-experts models, or models up to trillions of parameters; no audit shares comparable to V1.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose analysis, or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.

The study examines vision models and proxy interpretability metrics, not the essay's InceptionV1-sized estimates or a percentage of interpretable neurons. It does not establish that better explanation tools raise the share of interpretable neurons.
No test of whether attribution graphs built from a large language model's own neurons explain its behaviour without a replacement model or reconstruction error.
No test of whether an explanation fitted to activating examples predicts where the neuron fires on held-out examples.
No automated neuron-explanation scores based on simulating activations on new text, or finding that only a minority of neurons score well.

source_check.notes: Tab G.1/G.2 values match but are single runs with no error bars; Fig 5c gives SE over eight runs for dropout only. Fig 5b results (r1, r2, r4) are figure-only, come from pre-trained full-ImageNet models including ViTs, and the ResNet18 explanation is hedged. Supp G.2 prose lists ResNet18 among the trained models, but the tables show ResNet34, and the rows follow the tables. Dropout also raises VGG redundancy.

statements.correction: 2501.05398: L1 sparsity (lambda=80 vs 0) raises clarity at fixed model size (ResNet34 45.0->60.2, ResNet50 47.7->56.4, VGG-13 41.8->52.1, VGG-13 (BN) 35.6->48.0). Separately the study reports 'smaller and less performant convolutional models show lower interpretability', e.g. narrow ResNet18 is more polysemantic (figure-only).
statements.problem: SemanticLens numbers match Tab G.2. But 'not model size' misreads this study. The L1 experiment holds size fixed, and the same paper reports smaller/narrower pre-trained models as less interpretable (Fig 5 caption; Sec 4.4.2).
SemanticLens part is right. The authors hedge that the basis 'might be too small'. 'Wider models tend to have' monosemantic components is stated for models in general, not only ResNets (line ~1095).
SemanticLens part correct (ResNet higher clarity than ViT, ReLU credited, figure-only)

statements.correction: Dropout (40%) in VGG raises clarity (VGG-13 41.8->47.1; VGG-13 (BN) 35.5->39.6) but also raises redundancy (VGG-13 81.6->85.1; VGG-13 (BN) 79.1->81.6). Fig 5 caption: dropout gives more redundancies besides improved clarity, while sparsity improves interpretability overall. ResNets barely change.
statements.problem: All Tab G.1/G.2 numbers match. But 'dropout improves rather than degrades interpretability' leaves out that dropout also raises VGG redundancy. The authors contrast dropout with sparsity, which alone 'improves interpretability overall'.
SemanticLens side correct; ReLU attribution is the authors' explanation, not a tested swap

statements.correction: L1 and dropout results: ResNet34/50 and VGG-13 (+BN) trained on a 26-class ImageNet subset. ViT-vs-ResNet and ResNet18 results: pre-trained ImageNet models (timm/torchvision, including ViT-S/M/L), figure-only (Fig 5b). All use DINOv2 embeddings of penultimate-layer neurons.
statements.problem: Numbers match. But 'Measured ... on ImageNet-subset CNNs' is wrong for the ViT/ResNet and ResNet18 results (r1, r2, r4). Those come from pre-trained full-ImageNet models that include ViTs. 'Wider ResNets' is stated as 'wider models' and is unquantified.
